lead: A function is a rule that gives exactly one output for each allowed input. Its graph turns that rule into a picture, so you can see where it rises, falls, or repeats. Engineers read such pictures before they trust a formula: a voltage curve, a cost curve, a sensor reading. New functions often come from old ones by shifting, stretching, reflecting, composing, or inverting. This chapter builds that vocabulary and the habits for reading a graph, not just a formula.

sections.h3: A function gives one output per input

blocks.text: Function. A function f from a set A to a set B assigns exactly one element f(x) in B to each x in A. The set A is the domain: the allowed inputs. The set of actual values f(x) is the range. The codomain B is the declared output set; the range may be smaller.

Graph. The graph of f is the set of points (x, f(x)) in the xy-plane. Read x along the horizontal axis and y along the vertical axis. A curve is the graph of a function if every vertical line meets it at most once. This is the vertical line test. A circle fails it.

Piecewise and standard functions. A piecewise function uses different formulas on different parts of its domain. The absolute value |x| equals x for x≥0 and −x for x<0. Standard building blocks include constant, linear, quadratic, polynomial, rational, square-root, trigonometric, exponential and logarithmic functions.

Why it exists. Many engineering quantities depend on another quantity: cost depends on units produced, voltage on time, distance on speed. A function records that dependence in a form you can calculate and draw.
Start with y=f(x). Each change below makes a new function.

items: y=f(x)+k: move up k when k>0, down when k<0.
y=f(x−h): move right h when h>0, left when h<0. Inside changes act opposite to the sign.
y=a f(x): vertical stretch by |a|. If a<0, reflect about the x-axis.
y=f(bx): horizontal compression by 1/|b| when |b|>1, stretch when 0<|b|<1. If b<0, reflect about the y-axis.

blocks.where: y is the output; x is the input; a is the vertical stretch factor; b is the horizontal scale factor; h is the horizontal shift; k is the vertical shift.

blocks.text: For y=a f(b(x−h))+k, apply the inside changes (b and h) before the outside changes (a and k). A common error is to shift before scaling when the formula has b outside. Example: y=2(x−3)²+4 is x² shifted right 3, stretched vertically by 2, then shifted up 4. Its vertex is (3,4).
The derivative in 1.3 is another way to build a new function from an old one.

Composition. The composition (f∘g)(x)=f(g(x)) works from inside out. The domain needs x in the domain of g, and g(x) in the domain of f. Example: f(x)=√x and g(x)=x−3 give (f∘g)(x)=√(x−3), with domain x≥3.

Inverse. If f is one-to-one, its inverse f⁻¹ satisfies f⁻¹(f(x))=x and f(f⁻¹(y))=y. The graph of f⁻¹ is the reflection of the graph of f in the line y=x. Domain and range swap. f⁻¹(x) is not 1/f(x). f(x)=x² on x≥0 has inverse f⁻¹(x)=√x; on all real x it has no inverse because f(2)=f(−2).

figure.caption: Two parabolas with the same shape: y = x² and y = (x−2)²+1. The second one is the first moved 2 units right and 1 unit up; its vertex is (2,1).

spec.aria: Two parabolas: the grey y = x² and the blue y = (x−2)²+1, the same curve shifted two right and one up.

examples.question: Let f(x)=x². For y=f(x−2)+1, state the transformation, the vertex, the domain and the range. Sketch the graph.
steps: Start with f(x)=x². Its vertex is (0,0); domain is all real x; range is [0,∞).
Replace x by x−2: f(x−2)=(x−2)². At x=2 this gives 0, the old value at x=0, so the graph moves right by 2 units.
Add 1: y=(x−2)²+1. Every output rises by 1, so the graph moves up by 1 unit.
Vertex: (0,0) moves right 2 and up 1, giving (2,1). The parabola opens upward.
Domain: no new restriction, so all real x. Range: (x−2)²≥0, so y≥1; in interval form [1,∞).
Check points: x=1 and x=3 give y=2; x=0 gives y=5. Sketch through these points with vertex (2,1).
examples.answer: The graph is y=x² moved 2 units right and 1 unit up; vertex (2,1); domain = all real numbers; range = [1,∞).

k = 1.0

traps: f(x−2) moves the graph right by 2; f(x+2) moves it left by 2. Inside changes act opposite to the sign.
f⁻¹(x) is the inverse function, not 1/f(x). The reciprocal is a different function.
A circle is not the graph of a function because a vertical line can meet it twice. Use the vertical line test before finding domain or range.
For composition f(g(x)), x must be in the domain of g, and g(x) must be in the domain of f. Both conditions are needed.
The examiner's favourite question is to compare y=f(x−2) with y=f(x)+2: one moves right, the other moves up.

quiz.q: Define the domain and the range of a function f.
quiz.a: The domain is the set of allowed inputs x. The range is the set of actual outputs f(x).

quiz.q: Why does y=f(x−4) move the graph of f right by 4 units?
quiz.a: At x=4, f(x−4)=f(0). The old point at x=0 appears at x=4, so every point moves right by 4.

quiz.q: For f(x)=√x, state the domain and range of y=f(x−3)+2.
quiz.a: x−3≥0 gives x≥3, so the domain is [3,∞). The square root is ≥0, then add 2, so the range is [2,∞).
Stretch vertically by 2, reflect about the x-axis, then shift up by 3.

quiz.q: A graph fails the vertical line test at x=1: the line meets the curve at two points. Is the curve the graph of a function? Explain.
quiz.a: No. At x=1 the rule would give two outputs, but a function gives exactly one output for each allowed input.

quiz.q: Why does f(x)=x² on all real x have no inverse? How can you restrict it?
quiz.a: It is not one-to-one: f(2)=f(−2)=4. Restrict the domain to x≥0; then the inverse is f⁻¹(x)=√x.

quiz.q: Let f(x)=2x+1 and g(x)=x². Find (f∘g)(3) and (g∘f)(3).

beyond: Not for the exam. Transformations are the grammar of computer graphics: a sprite's position is a translation, its size a scale, and a mirror a reflection. In data science, log and square-root transforms change the shape of a distribution before fitting a model. In control engineering, composing a sensor function with a controller function is routine. Search for 'function transformations', 'composition of functions domain', and 'inverse function theorem'.
